trial_name: VICTAS — Vitamin C, Thiamine, and Hydrocortisone in Sepsis (2021)
citation: Sevransky JE, Rothman RE, Hager DN, Bernard GR, Brown SM, Buchman TG, et al. Effect of Vitamin C, Thiamine, and Hydrocortisone on Ventilator- and Vasopressor-Free Days in Patients With Sepsis: The VICTAS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021;325(8):742-750
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, adaptive, superiority
one_liner: In ICU sepsis with respiratory/cardiovascular dysfunction, combination IV vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisone did not increase ventilator- and vasopressor-free days at 30 days compared with placebo (median 25 vs 26 days; P=0.85), with no supportive benefit across secondary outcomes.

pico.population: Adults ≥18 years with suspected infection and sepsis-induced acute respiratory and/or cardiovascular dysfunction requiring ICU admission, randomised within 24 hours of meeting organ dysfunction criteria
pico.intervention: IV vitamin C 1.5 g + thiamine 100 mg + hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours for up to 96 hours (or until ICU discharge/death), started within 4 hours of randomisation
pico.comparison: Matching IV placebo every 6 hours on the same schedule and duration, with identical withholding rules (study hydrocortisone/placebo withheld if open-label corticosteroids reached ≥200 mg/day hydrocortisone-equivalent)
pico.outcome: Ventilator- and vasopressor-free days (VVFDs) through day 30 (primary)

background.existing_knowledge: High-dose IV vitamin C, thiamine, and hydrocortisone (‘HAT therapy’) gained attention after a retrospective before–after study reported large mortality reductions in septic shock. Vitamin C monotherapy trials in ARDS/sepsis showed biologic effects but unclear clinical benefit.
background.knowledge_gap: Subsequent RCTs of combination regimens (with or without hydrocortisone) yielded neutral results, leaving equipoise regarding efficacy, optimal timing, and component-specific effects.
background.hypothesis: Early IV vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisone would increase VVFDs through day 30 compared with placebo in adults with sepsis-induced organ dysfunction.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, adaptive sample-size trial (planned maximum N=2000) in 43 US hospitals; patients enrolled from ED or ICU.
methods.setting: 43 hospitals in the United States; enrolled August 2018 to January 2020 (administratively terminated after 501 patients).

inclusion: Suspected infection (blood culture ordered AND antibiotics initiated)
Acute respiratory dysfunction: PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 or SpO2/FiO2 ≤315, AND requiring invasive ventilation, NIPPV, or HFNC ≥40 L/min with FiO2 ≥0.40 (persistent at randomisation)
Acute cardiovascular dysfunction: any vasopressor >1 hour to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg despite ≥1 L crystalloid (persistent at randomisation)
Randomised within 24 hours of meeting organ dysfunction criteria
exclusion: Not fully enumerated in main report (refer to published protocol)

methods.intervention: Vitamin C 1.5 g IV + thiamine 100 mg IV + hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h, started within 4 hours of randomisation, continued up to 96 hours or until ICU discharge/death. Study hydrocortisone withheld if open-label corticosteroids reached ≥200 mg/day hydrocortisone-equivalent.
methods.comparison: Matching placebo IV q6h on same schedule, with identical withholding rules for open-label corticosteroids.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (participants, clinicians, investigators, outcome assessors); investigational pharmacies prepared masked study kits.
methods.sample_size_power: Adaptive design maximum N=2000, targeting 1.5-day improvement in VVFDs (assuming ~25% 30-day mortality). Interim analyses at N=200/300/400 (stopping for ≥99% predictive probability of 30-day mortality benefit) and at N=500/1000/1500 (stopping for VVFD efficacy/futility). One-sided type I error controlled at 2.5%; primary VVFD hypothesis used one-sided P<0.022 after interim adjustment. Early termination due to administrative/funding reasons at N=501.
methods.primary_outcome: Ventilator- and vasopressor-free days (VVFDs) through day 30 (death assigned 0 VVFDs; last support status carried forward after discharge).
secondary_outcomes: 30-day all-cause mortality (gated – formal testing only if primary VVFD significant)
ICU and hospital length of stay
Delirium- and coma-free days through day 30
Kidney replacement therapy–free days through day 30
SOFA score change from baseline to day 4
methods.follow_up: Through day 30 for primary outcome; survival follow-up to day 180 (telephone).

headline_bullets: No improvement in primary outcome: VVFDs median 25 vs 26 days, median difference –1 day (95% CI –4 to 2), P=0.85
30-day mortality similar (22% vs 24%); not formally tested due to gatekeeping
No supportive trends across any exploratory outcome (ICU/hospital LOS, delirium/coma-free days, RRT-free days, SOFA change, 180-day mortality)
Per-protocol analysis also neutral (median VVFDs 26 vs 26 days; difference 0, 95% CI –3 to 2)

outcomes_table.note: One-sided hypothesis, interim-adjusted α; death = 0 VVFDs
Gated – formal testing not performed because primary VVFD was not significant

outcomes_table.outcome: Time to ICU discharge, median days (IQR)
Time to hospital discharge, median days (IQR)
Delirium- and coma-free days through day 30, median (IQR)
outcomes_table.note: Exploratory; low medians reflect high delirium/coma burden even among survivors

outcomes_table.outcome: SOFA score change (baseline to day 4), median (IQR)
outcomes_table.note: Exploratory; directionality as defined in the report

safety: 2 adverse events judged possibly related to study drug in intervention arm (haemorrhagic shock; worsening kidney function)
No serious adverse events judged related to study treatment

High-dose vitamin C can cause spuriously elevated point-of-care glucose readings with some meters; VICTAS used a validated glucose meter unaffected by high vitamin C, which is important for internal validity and patient safety

domains.notes: Central randomisation 1:1, stratified by site; allocation concealed via numbered study kits prepared by investigational pharmacies.
Double-blind design; primary and most secondary outcomes objective (death, organ support, discharge), reducing detection bias.

501 randomised, all included in main ITT analyses. 180-day mortality observed in 457/501 (91%) for observed-status analysis; incomplete follow-up could introduce bias if non-random. Per-protocol populations: 212/252 (84.1%) intervention vs 205/249 (82.3%) placebo; moderate protocol deviations but similar between arms.

Study hydrocortisone/placebo was withheld if open-label corticosteroids exceeded ≥200 mg/day; open-label corticosteroid use was 33.0% (intervention) vs 32.1% (placebo), partially attenuating the separation of the hydrocortisone component. Withholding rules applied equally to both arms.
Similar severity: median SOFA 9 (IQR 6–12) in both arms; 44% in each arm had both respiratory and cardiovascular dysfunction; median time from meeting criteria to randomisation 15 vs 14 hours.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity appears moderate-to-strong given robust randomisation/blinding, objective endpoints, and reasonable protocol delivery; the principal threat is early administrative termination (reduced precision and altered operating characteristics) alongside partial corticosteroid ‘contamination’ from open-label use.

domains.notes: ICU-level adults with suspected infection and vasopressor/advanced respiratory support, broadly reflecting moderate–severe sepsis in high-income settings.

Regimen uses globally available drugs; however, q6-hourly dosing and need for glucose meters unaffected by high-dose vitamin C may challenge resource-limited settings. Exclusion of patients not requiring ICU admission limits applicability to ward/ED-only sepsis.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate for ICU sepsis populations requiring organ support; translation to non-ICU settings or systems without robust medication-delivery and glucose-monitoring infrastructure is more limited.

strengths: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre design across 43 hospitals
Patient-centred primary endpoint integrating survival and freedom from key organ supports (ventilation/vasopressors)
Prespecified adaptive design with multiplicity control (interim-adjusted α; gatekeeping for mortality)
limitations: Stopped early for administrative/funding reasons (N=501 vs planned N=2000), reducing precision and leaving residual uncertainty about smaller effects
Open-label corticosteroid use in ~1/3 of patients in both arms, potentially attenuating the hydrocortisone component separation
Missing 180-day survival status in a subset, with analyses using observed-status, risking bias if missingness is non-random

critical_appraisal.summary: VICTAS is a well-designed but underpowered test of metabolic resuscitation in sepsis; early termination and partial steroid contamination weaken confidence that even a small benefit would have been detected, but the complete lack of signal across all endpoints, corroborated by external RCTs, supports a conclusion of no clinically meaningful benefit.
strengths: Rigorous blinding and objective endpoints minimised bias
Adaptive design with prespecified stopping rules and multiplicity control
Broad multicentre enrolment enhances external validity
weaknesses: Early administrative termination severely reduced power (post hoc conditional probability of success only 30.7%)
Open-label corticosteroid use in ~33% of patients blurred the hydrocortisone separation
Incomplete 180-day follow-up and reliance on observed-status analysis

sections.authors_conclusion: VICTAS provides no support for routine use of combined vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisone to increase organ-support–free days in ICU sepsis. Given workflow burden and safety considerations, off-label use should be avoided outside trials or structured protocols with appropriate monitoring.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not use vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisone to improve organ-support-free days in ICU sepsis; no benefit was seen, and potential safety issues (e.g., glucometry interference) plus q6h dosing burden argue against routine use.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: ICU patients with sepsis and acute respiratory or cardiovascular dysfunction requiring organ support.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: This does not rule out a benefit in highly selected subgroups (e.g., measured vitamin C deficiency), but such benefit remains unproven. The trial did not find harm, but absence of benefit plus safety concerns support de-implementation.
implementation_caveats: Requires q6-hourly IV dosing for up to 96 hours
Must use glucose meters validated to avoid interference with high-dose vitamin C (some point-of-care devices give falsely elevated readings)
Study hydrocortisone was withheld when open-label corticosteroids exceeded 200 mg/day; in settings where corticosteroids are standard, this may alter the effective dose of the combination

controversies.topic: Early administrative termination and funding transparency
controversies.notes: A JAMA editor’s note highlighted concerns about funding decisions and DSMB membership disclosures in VICTAS, emphasising the importance of trial governance in publicly funded critical care RCTs.

controversies.topic: Safety of high-dose vitamin C with glucometry
controversies.notes: High-dose vitamin C can cause falsely elevated point-of-care glucose readings, risking inappropriate insulin administration and hypoglycaemia; VICTAS mitigated this by using a validated device, but this remains a major implementation issue.

Multiple subsequent RCTs and meta-analyses (including LOVIT, VITAMINS, ATLAS) have uniformly shown no benefit for vitamin C–based regimens in sepsis; VICTAS’s neutral result aligns with this body of evidence.

Major sepsis guidelines recommend against routine IV vitamin C in sepsis, and a rapid practice guideline on IV vitamin C in critically ill adults similarly advises against routine use outside research.

context_related_trials.relation: The initial retrospective report that sparked interest in HAT therapy, showing large mortality reductions; subsequent prospective RCTs (including VICTAS) did not confirm benefit.

Vitamin C monotherapy in ARDS; suggested secondary benefits but no clear improvement in primary outcome, raising multiplicity concerns and prompting further investigation in combination trials like VICTAS.
Open-label RCT of vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisone vs hydrocortisone alone in septic shock; found no improvement in vasopressor-free days or mortality, consistent with VICTAS.
RCT testing a similar vitamin C–based combination in sepsis; results aligned with VICTAS in showing no benefit.

Large RCT of high-dose IV vitamin C monotherapy in ICU sepsis; showed no improvement and raised concern for potential harm on a composite organ-dysfunction endpoint, further undermining the case for vitamin C–based strategies.

unresolved_questions: Could a subset with true vitamin C deficiency benefit from replacement?
Is there a role for earlier initiation (pre-ICU) or longer duration?
Do specific host phenotypes (e.g., hyperinflammation) derive benefit, and can they be identified at the bedside?

numbers_to_remember: Primary VVFDs median 25 vs 26 days (difference -1 day, P=0.85)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: VICTAS definitively shows no benefit from vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisone in ICU sepsis and supports guideline recommendations against routine use.
